def: Keeping identical copies of some state on several machines so that the loss of one machine does not lose the state.
A design where identical deterministic state machines on several servers process the same commands in the same order, so they compute identical copies of the same state.
The one server in a cluster that is currently in charge of deciding the order of operations.
The problem of getting a set of servers to agree on a single value, or a single sequence of values, despite failures and an unreliable network.
The explicit list of failures a protocol is designed to tolerate, and the failures it assumes never happen.
A network failure that splits the servers into groups that can talk within the group but not across groups.
A fault model where servers fail by stopping and may later restart, reloading their saved state and rejoining the system.
A fault model where failed servers may behave arbitrarily, including sending false or contradictory information.
The servers in a cluster that accept the leader's decisions and replicate its state.
Small periodic messages a leader sends to followers to signal that it is still alive and in charge.
A failure state in which two servers in one cluster simultaneously believe they are the leader.
Invalidating a stale leader's actions by attaching a number or timestamp to every decision and rejecting decisions that carry a stale one.
The 1985 proof that in a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee that it terminates if even one server may crash.
A system model that assumes timing is not fully arbitrary, only that message delays and processing times eventually stay within some loose bound.
The average time a machine or system runs before its next failure.
More than half of the servers in a cluster.
The minimum number of servers that must agree for a cluster decision to count.
The property that any two majorities of a cluster must share at least one common server.
State kept only in memory, such as the commit index and last applied index, which is lost when the process exits and reconstructed on restart.
State stored on some medium that survives a process crash and reboot.
Storage that survives crashes, typically a local disk with appropriate sync operations, though the Raft paper deliberately abstracts over the exact mechanism.
Durable state that the protocol explicitly writes so it can be reloaded after a restart.
A system call that forces all modified data and metadata for a file out to the underlying storage device, establishing an ordering boundary.
An append-only sequence of records describing operations that must be applied to the state machine; the source of truth from which the state machine is rebuilt.
The kernel's in-memory cache of file contents; writes normally go here first and are flushed to disk later.
Volatile memory on the disk controller or drive itself that can buffer writes and lose them if power fails before the cache is flushed.
Like fsync, but forces only data and a subset of metadata, omitting metadata not required for later reads of the file contents.
The act of reading a log after a crash and reapplying its entries to rebuild state.
An operation that produces the same result no matter how many times it is applied, so replaying it is safe.
